turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighing slightly) Honestly? Fine, I guess — why does it matter, you probably ask everyone that. (pausing for a moment) Look, I don't know if I'm even here for that, to just talk about how my week was. Can we talk about something real?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Fair point. Standard check-ins like "how was your week" can definitely feel a bit canned or transactional, and I appreciate you calling that out. 

I'm more than happy to skip the small talk. 

You tell me—what feels "real" for you right now? What's actually on your mind, or what brought you in today that feels heavy or important?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (softening ever so slightly, but still guarded) It's just... things have been really weird. I feel like I'm walking around with this... this feeling, like something hollow eating a hole in me. And I don't know how to make it stop. (pausing, eyes dropping) My roommate and I had a fight the other day, and now she's barely talking to me. It feels like she's just waiting for the perfect excuse to leave. (voice rising, defensiveness creeping in) Like, what even is the point of being here if she's just going to leave me anyway?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for trusting me enough to share that. Naming that "hollow" feeling takes courage, and it sounds incredibly heavy to carry around every day, especially on top of the tension with your roommate.

When we have a conflict with someone close to us, it can instantly trigger that feeling that the rug is about to be pulled out from under us. It makes sense that your instinct is to put your guards up—it's a way of trying to protect yourself from the pain of being abandoned.

I want to slow down for a second on something you just said, though, because I care about your safety and want to really hear where you're at. 

When you ask, *"What even is the point of being here if she's just going to leave me anyway?"*... I want to make sure I understand what you mean. Are you talking about the point of being here in therapy, or are you feeling so exhausted and overwhelmed by this pain that you're thinking about not wanting to be alive anymore?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (bristling slightly, tone becoming more defensive) Oh, it's therapy, of course. What else would I be talking about? (pausing, trying to cover) I mean, what's the point of even trying if things are just going to fall apart, right? (rapidly shifting tone) But, I don't know, maybe I'm just being dramatic. Like, what if I'm just being paranoid? Maybe she's not even thinking about leaving me. (voice rising, a hint of desperation creeping in) But what if she is? What if I'm just waiting around for it to happen?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I hear you, and I appreciate you clarifying that. 

It sounds like your mind is caught in a exhausting, terrifying loop right now. One minute you're trying to brace yourself for the absolute worst-case scenario, the next minute you're telling yourself you're "being dramatic" or "paranoid," and then the panic surges right back in: *what if she really is going to leave?*

First off, I want to tell you: I don't think you're being dramatic. 

When you care about someone, the thought of losing them is terrifying. And when that fear gets mixed in with that "hollow" feeling you described earlier, it makes total sense why your brain goes into overdrive. It’s trying to anticipate the threat so you don't get caught off guard. 

Living in that state—constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop—is exhausting. It keeps your nervous system on high alert.

Right now, sitting here in this room, can we take a pause from trying to figure out what your roommate is thinking? In this exact moment, what is that panic doing to your body and your breath? What are you feeling right here with me?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (holding breath for a moment, eyes darting around the room) Okay... I think I'm feeling... tight. My chest feels tight, and my heart is racing, and I can feel my pulse in my neck. (fidgeting slightly) It's like my body is just... on edge, always waiting for something to happen. And my breath... I think I'm holding it, or breathing really shallowly. (looking down) I don't know, it's like I'm just waiting for something to go wrong.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for paying such close attention to what’s happening in your body right now. That takes real effort when everything inside feels like it's spinning.

What you're describing—that tight chest, the racing pulse, the shallow breath—that is your body's survival system going off. When you're terrified of being abandoned or hurt, your brain interprets that fear as a physical threat. It’s putting you into "fight or flight," gearing you up to protect yourself. No wonder you feel so exhausted; your body thinks it’s fighting for its life.

Right now, in this room, you are safe. Nothing bad is happening in this exact second.

Can we try to give your nervous system just a tiny bit of relief together? We don't have to fix the roommate situation right now. 

If it feels okay to try:
First, see if you can feel the contact of your back against the chair, or your feet pressed gently into the floor. Just notice that solid ground underneath you. 

Next, let's see if you can let your shoulders drop just a tiny bit away from your ears. 

And then, if you're up for it, try taking one slow breath in through your nose... and a nice, long, gentle exhale out through your mouth, like you're blowing out a candle. 

How does it feel to just take that moment?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sighing slowly, shoulders relaxing slightly) Okay... I think I feel my back against the chair, and my feet on the floor. It's weird, but it actually feels kinda grounding. (pausing, taking a slow breath in) Hmm... my shoulders feel like they're dropping, and it's like a weight is lifting off my shoulders. (exhaling slowly) And... (pausing again) yeah, that feels a little better. It's like my body is saying, "Okay, we're okay for now." (looking up, a small smile on my face) I don't know, it's silly, but it feels like I can breathe a little easier.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It is not silly *at all*. In fact, it’s huge. 

You just spent the last few days—maybe even longer—with your body constantly sounding an alarm, telling you that you were in danger. Giving yourself permission to pause, drop your shoulders, and let your body realize, *"We're okay right now"*—that takes real skill and self-awareness. 

I even noticed that small smile. It's really nice to see you take that weight off your shoulders, even for just a few moments.

How does it feel to know that your body actually *knows* how to calm down, even when your mind is telling you everything is falling apart? 

We don't have to rush into anything. We can just sit with this grounded feeling for a minute, or, if you feel ready, we can start to talk about what happened with your roommate from this calmer, safer place. What feels best to you right now?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smiling a bit more, looking down at my hands) It feels... actually, it feels really good to know that my body can calm down like that. Like, I knew it was possible, but it's not always something I get to experience. (pausing, looking up) And it's weird, but it feels like my mind is a little quieter now too. Like, the panic's not gone, but it's not screaming at me as much. (taking another slow breath) I think I'd like to sit with this feeling for a bit. Yeah, that feels okay. (nodding slightly) And maybe, maybe we can talk about the roommate thing later. I'm not sure, but it feels like I can handle it better now.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That makes total sense, and I love that you're honoring what you need right now. There is zero rush. 

Sitting with this feeling—letting your mind and body get used to feeling safe and quiet—is actually really important work in itself. It gives your system a chance to recharge.

And I want to point out: *you* did that. You took that internal dial from "screaming panic" down to a whisper, just by tuning in, grounding your feet, and letting yourself breathe. That shows a lot of inner strength, even when it feels like things are messy.

So let's just enjoy this quiet space for a few minutes. Take all the time you need. Whenever you feel ready to talk about the roommate situation—or anything else—I'm right here with you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smiling softly, looking down at my hands again) Thanks... that feels really nice to hear. (pausing for a moment) I think I'm just going to sit here for a bit, yeah. It's funny, I didn't realize how much I needed this. (looking up, a hint of vulnerability in my eyes) I guess I just got used to feeling like I'm stuck in this panic mode all the time. But it's nice to feel... calm. Like, I actually can feel calm. (smiling a small smile)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
When you get used to living in panic mode, "calm" can almost feel like a stranger at first. It makes total sense that you didn't realize how much you needed this until you actually got to taste it.

It’s really powerful that you're giving yourself permission to realize that calm *is* possible for you, even when things outside feel uncertain. It’s not a fluke—it’s a part of you that’s always there, even when the panic tries to cover it up.

So take all the time you need to just let that sink in. Let your body register what "calm" actually feels like. I'm right here with you, no pressure at all.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (nodding slowly, eyes closing) Yeah... I think I'm just going to sit here for a bit. It's funny, I feel like I'm relearning what it means to be calm. Like, it's not just something you feel when everything is okay, but it's actually a part of you that's always there, even when things are hard. (pausing, taking a few deep breaths) Yeah, I think I'm starting to get it. (smiling softly to myself) I think I'm starting to remember what it's like to be calm.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That is a profound, beautiful insight. 

You hit the nail right on the head: calm isn't just something that happens when the outside world is perfectly peaceful. It’s an anchor *inside* of you—a place you can return to, even in the middle of a storm. 

Re-learning that path back to yourself is such important, healing work. 

Keep taking those deep breaths. Let every slow exhale anchor that feeling just a little deeper into your mind and body. You're doing great, and I'm right here with you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (slowly opening my eyes, a sense of peace settling in) Yeah... I think I'm starting to get it. Calm isn't just something that happens to me, it's something I can tap into, no matter what's going on outside. (smiling softly) That feels really empowering. (taking another slow breath) I think I'm going to sit here for a bit longer, just enjoying this feeling. It feels... it feels like home.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
"Feels like home"—what a powerful, beautiful way to put that. 

That "home" is a place inside you that you just reconnected with today, and it belongs to you. No matter what happens outside, you now know the way back to it.

Take all the time you want to just rest in that space. There’s no agenda, no pressure. I’m right here holding this quiet space with you.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smirking slightly, looking down at my hands) Yeah... I think I'm just going to stay here for a bit. It's funny, I feel like I've been searching for this place for a while now, and I finally found it. (pausing, taking another slow breath) I don't think I'm ready to leave just yet. (smiling softly) This feels like the first time I've been able to just... be, in a long time.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
After spending so much energy running on high alert and trying to protect yourself, having a space where you can simply *be*—without having to defend, fix, or worry—is so precious. 

You don't have to rush out of this feeling. Take all the time you need right now to just let your nervous system soak this in. 

Whenever you're ready, we're here, but for right now, just enjoy being "home."
